questions.q: Compute the first few partial quotients of $\pi=3.14159265\ldots$ The expansion begins $[a_0;a_1,a_2,a_3,\ldots]$ with $a_0=3$, $a_1=7$, $a_2=15$, $a_3=1$. What is the convergent $p_3/q_3$ as a fraction (enter the numerator $p_3$)?
questions.explain: The recursion $p_n=a_n p_{n-1}+p_{n-2}$, $q_n=a_n q_{n-1}+q_{n-2}$ with $p_{-1}=1, p_0=3$ and $q_{-1}=0, q_0=1$ gives $p_1=22, q_1=7$ (so $22/7$), then $p_2=333, q_2=106$, then $p_3=355, q_3=113$. The famous approximation $355/113$ is accurate to seven decimal places — far better than $q^{-2}$ would predict, because $a_4=292$ is large.

questions.q: Lagrange's theorem characterises which real numbers as having an eventually periodic continued fraction?
choices: exactly the real quadratic irrationals (degree-2 algebraic over $\mathbb{Q}$)
questions.explain: Rationals have terminating expansions; transcendental numbers have aperiodic expansions of unknown structure (no pattern is known for $\pi$ or $e^2$). The continued fraction of $\alpha$ is eventually periodic iff $\alpha$ satisfies a quadratic equation over $\mathbb{Q}$ — for example $\sqrt{2}=[1;\overline{2}]$ and $\varphi=[\overline{1}]$.

choices: If $p/q$ is any rational with $0<q<q_n$, then $|q\alpha-p|>|q_n\alpha-p_n|$ — no rational of smaller denominator gets closer in the weighted sense.
They are the only rationals with $|\alpha-p/q|<1/q^2$.
They are the unique rationals $p/q$ with $q$ a Fibonacci number.
questions.explain: The 'best approximation' property is in the weighted form $|q\alpha-p|$: no rational with denominator strictly smaller than $q_n$ comes closer in this sense. This is stronger than option 0 — any non-convergent fraction with comparable denominator is strictly further away.

questions.q: Hurwitz's theorem (1891) states: for every irrational $\alpha$, there are infinitely many $p/q\in\mathbb{Q}$ with $|\alpha-p/q|<C/q^2$. What is the optimal constant $C$?
questions.explain: Hurwitz's constant is $1/\sqrt{5}\approx 0.4472$. Replacing it by anything smaller fails for the golden ratio $\varphi=(1+\sqrt{5})/2$, which is the extremal irrational. Restricting to irrationals not equivalent to $\varphi$ (i.e. without $1$s in the tail) lets you push the constant down to $1/\sqrt{8}$ (Markoff).

questions.q: The golden ratio $\varphi=(1+\sqrt{5})/2$ has the slowest possible convergent approximation. For its $n$-th convergent $p_n/q_n=F_{n+1}/F_n$ (Fibonacci ratios), the error satisfies $q_n^2|\varphi-p_n/q_n|\to 1/\sqrt{5}$. What is this limit numerically (3 decimals)?
questions.explain: $1/\sqrt{5}\approx 0.4472$. So $q_n^2|\varphi-p_n/q_n|$ never drops far below $0.447$ — pictorially the golden ratio sits exactly on the boundary of Hurwitz's bound. Every other irrational has at least one tail value of $a_i\ge 2$ in its continued fraction, which lets it occasionally do better.

questions.q: Which of the following continued-fraction tails describe an irrational that achieves the worst-case Hurwitz bound (constant $\sqrt{5}$)?
questions.explain: Hurwitz's constant $\sqrt{5}$ is achieved exactly on the $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$-orbit of $\varphi$ — i.e. irrationals whose continued-fraction tail is eventually $1,1,1,\ldots$. Quadratic irrationals like $\sqrt{2}$ and $\sqrt{10}$ have tails containing $a_i\ge 2$, so they enjoy infinitely many approximations strictly better than $1/(\sqrt{5}q^2)$.

questions.q: Liouville's bound says: if $\alpha$ is algebraic of degree $d$ with minimal polynomial $m(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$, then for every $p/q\ne\alpha$,
questions.explain: The proof uses $|m(p/q)|\ge 1/q^d$ (since $q^d m(p/q)\in\mathbb{Z}$ is non-zero) combined with the mean-value bound $|m(p/q)|\le M\cdot|\alpha-p/q|$ for $M=\sup|m'|$ near $\alpha$. So $|\alpha-p/q|\ge 1/(M q^d)$. The key feature: the exponent $d$ is the algebraic degree.

questions.q: Liouville's constant is the explicit transcendental $L=\sum_{n=1}^\infty 10^{-n!}$. Its truncation $L_k=\sum_{n=1}^k 10^{-n!}$ has the form $p_k/q_k$ with $q_k=10^{k!}$. What is the rational error exponent $r_k$ defined by $|L-L_k|<q_k^{-r_k}$, in the limit $k\to\infty$? (Enter $\infty$ as a large number, say 999.)
questions.explain: $|L-L_k|<2\cdot 10^{-(k+1)!}$ and $q_k^n=10^{n\cdot k!}$. So $|L-L_k|<q_k^{-r_k}$ holds iff $r_k\le (k+1)!/k!-\epsilon = k+1-\epsilon$. The rational exponent $r_k\to\infty$, violating Liouville's bound for any algebraic degree $d$. So $L$ is transcendental — the first known transcendental, exhibited by Liouville in 1844, three decades before Hermite's $e$.

questions.q: What is the contradiction Liouville extracts from a number $\alpha$ admitting infinitely many rationals with $|\alpha-p/q|<q^{-n}$ for arbitrary $n$?
choices: If $\alpha$ were algebraic of degree $d$, then $|\alpha-p/q|>C/q^d$, but the assumption gives $|\alpha-p/q|<q^{-n}<C/q^d$ for $n>d$ and $q$ large — contradiction. So $\alpha$ is transcendental.
questions.explain: The whole proof is a clean contrapositive of Liouville's bound. Algebraic numbers cannot be approximated arbitrarily well in the polynomial-rate sense; any $\alpha$ that beats every polynomial rate must be transcendental. This was the first transcendence proof — predating Hermite ($e$, 1873) and Lindemann ($\pi$, 1882).

questions.q: Roth's theorem (1955) states: for every algebraic irrational $\alpha$ and every $\varepsilon>0$, there are only finitely many $p/q\in\mathbb{Q}$ with
questions.explain: Roth replaced Liouville's exponent $d$ by the universal $2+\varepsilon$, independent of degree. The exponent $2$ is sharp: Dirichlet's theorem produces infinitely many $p/q$ with $|\alpha-p/q|<q^{-2}$ for every irrational. So Roth's bound is the best possible polynomial-rate statement.

choices: Because the proof uses non-constructive logic (axiom of choice).

Because the proof yields a bound on the NUMBER of exceptional $p/q$ but not on their SIZE — given $\alpha$ and $\varepsilon$, no algorithm currently produces a $Q_0(\alpha,\varepsilon)$ such that the bound holds for $q\ge Q_0$.
Because Roth could not compute a single example.
questions.explain: Roth's index argument bounds the count of exceptional approximations but cannot pin down where they lie. Effective versions (e.g. Baker's logarithmic forms) give weaker exponents but explicit $Q_0$. This trade-off is structural: Roth's theorem and Faltings' theorem on Mordell share the same effectiveness gap.

questions.q: Which of the following are TRUE about Roth's theorem and its descendants?
choices: The Schmidt subspace theorem (1972) generalises Roth to systems of linear forms in several variables.
Roth's theorem implies that the equation $x^n-2y^n=k$ has only finitely many integer solutions for $n\ge 3$, $k\ne 0$ (Thue–Roth).
Roth's theorem gives an effective algorithm to list all integer solutions of a Thue equation.
Roth's theorem applies to transcendental $\alpha$ as well as algebraic ones.
questions.explain: Schmidt's subspace theorem is the higher-dimensional sequel; Thue equations $F(x,y)=k$ for irreducible $F$ of degree $\ge 3$ have finitely many integer solutions by Roth. The theorem is ineffective (no algorithm — option 2 false), and transcendental $\alpha$ can be approximated to arbitrary order, so Roth fails for them (e.g. Liouville numbers — option 3 false).

The Markoff equation $x^2+y^2+z^2=3xyz$ has integer solutions $(1,1,1)$, $(1,1,2)$, $(1,2,5)$, $(1,5,13)$, $(2,5,29)$, ... All solutions form a tree generated by Vieta jumps $(x,y,z)\mapsto(x,y,3xy-z)$ from $(1,1,1)$. The Markoff numbers are the largest coordinates: $1,2,5,13,29,34,89,\ldots$

questions.q: Below the value $3$, the Lagrange spectrum is:
choices: a discrete set, namely $\{\sqrt{9-4/m^2}\}$ as $m$ runs over Markoff numbers
a Cantor set of measure zero
questions.explain: The spectrum starts at $\sqrt{5}$ (golden ratio), then jumps to $\sqrt{8}$ ($m=2$), $\sqrt{221}/5$ ($m=5$), $\sqrt{1517}/13$ ($m=13$), $\ldots$ accumulating at $3$. Above $3$, Hall (1947) showed the spectrum contains a half-line ("Hall's ray"), i.e. has positive Lebesgue measure.

questions.q: The smallest three Markoff numbers are $1, 2, 5$. What is the next one?
questions.explain: From $(1,2,5)$ the Vieta jump gives $(1,5, 3\cdot 1\cdot 5-2)=(1,5,13)$. The Markoff numbers $1,2,5,13,29,34,89,169,\ldots$ form OEIS sequence A002559. The famous open question is the unicity conjecture: each Markoff number determines its triple uniquely up to permutation.

questions.q: The Mahler–Ridout theorem extends Roth to which setting?
choices: Replacing the archimedean absolute value $|\cdot|_\infty$ by a $p$-adic absolute value $|\cdot|_p$, or mixing several places at once.
Replacing $\mathbb{Q}$ by $\mathbb{C}$ on the approximator side.
questions.explain: If $\alpha\in\mathbb{Q}_p$ is algebraic over $\mathbb{Q}$ and $\varepsilon>0$, then $|\alpha-p/q|_p>q^{-2-\varepsilon}$ for all but finitely many $p/q\in\mathbb{Q}$. The statement combines naturally with the archimedean Roth: one can demand simultaneous good approximation at finitely many places of $\mathbb{Q}$, and the count of exceptions is still finite.

questions.q: Schmidt's subspace theorem (1972) packages Roth in $n$ dimensions. The conclusion: for linearly independent linear forms $L_1,\ldots,L_n$ with algebraic coefficients and $\varepsilon>0$, the integer solutions of $|L_1(x)\cdots L_n(x)|<\|x\|^{-\varepsilon}$ in $\mathbb{Z}^n$ are
choices: contained in a finite union of proper rational subspaces of $\mathbb{Q}^n$
always lie on a single line
questions.explain: The conclusion is geometric: solutions concentrate on finitely many proper subspaces, each of which can be analysed inductively. The case $n=2$ recovers Roth (one form is $x_1-\alpha x_2$, the other is $x_2$); the higher-dimensional version proves finiteness of integer points on many varieties — the modern proof of Mordell's conjecture (Faltings) and the proof of the Mordell–Lang conjecture (Vojta, Faltings) ride on subspace-theorem-style ideas.

questions.q: Which problems are settled (or substantially attacked) by the subspace theorem?
choices: Finiteness of integral points on hyperbolic curves of genus $\ge 1$ (Siegel + refinements).
Effective bounds on solutions of Thue equations.
The Mordell–Lang conjecture for subvarieties of semiabelian varieties (Faltings, Vojta).
questions.explain: The subspace theorem is fundamentally non-effective (just like Roth), so option 1 is false. It powers Siegel-style finiteness results and Vojta–Faltings on Mordell–Lang. The Riemann hypothesis lives in a different world (analytic continuation, $\zeta$-zeros) and has no known link to Diophantine approximation.
